```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(afex)   # repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction, as in the original

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "sievers2012-pilot-a"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "sievers2012-phase2"
```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures.
#
# Sievers et al. (2013), US experiment, main text "United States: Results": multiway ANOVA on
# the slider positions, Emotion (5) x Slider (5) within subjects and Modality (music vs
# movement) between subjects, N = 50 (25 per modality), Greenhouse-Geisser corrected df.
# The key effect is the Emotion x Slider interaction. (The partial eta-squared of 0.23 in the
# cross-cultural section pools the US and Kreung samples and is not used here.)
original <- tibble(
  term = c("emotion:slider", "emotion", "condition", "condition:emotion", "condition:emotion:slider"),
  df1  = c(4.81, 2.97, 1, 2.97, 4.81),
  df2  = c(230.73, 142.44, 48, 142.44, 230.73),
  F    = c(112.90, 185.56, 4.66, 0.97, 4.50),
  pes  = c(0.70, 0.79, 0.09, 0.02, 0.09),
  N    = 50
)
original_n   <- c(music = 25, movement = 25)
original_key <- original |> filter(term == "emotion:slider")

# Mean raw slider settings by emotion, music and movement pooled: SI Table S1, "United States
# means". Slider names follow experiment.js: scale = consonance/smoothness, interval = step
# size, updown = direction (probability of a downward step).
original_means <- tribble(
  ~slider,    ~angry, ~happy, ~peaceful, ~sad,  ~scared,
  "bpm",      331.00, 280.12, 69.48,     53.74, 289.68,
  "jitter",   53.70,  33.24,  11.30,     19.44, 58.22,
  "scale",    8.00,   32.00,  32.34,     22.66, 10.08,
  "interval", 67.92,  49.36,  23.66,     26.28, 52.28,
  "updown",   76.94,  35.56,  38.34,     78.30, 51.12
) |> pivot_longer(-slider, names_to = "emotion", values_to = "mean")

# Slider ranges (same in the original and in experiment.js), for plotting on a common 0-1 scale.
slider_ranges <- tibble(
  slider = c("bpm", "jitter", "scale", "interval", "updown"),
  lo     = c(30, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  hi     = c(400, 99, 37, 100, 100),
  label  = c("Rate (per minute)", "Jitter", "Consonance / smoothness", "Step size (big/small)", "Direction (down)")
)
```

# Key statistics

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the Phase 2 row reports the new comparison: adapt its code and say so in the caption.
:::

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# How slider values are put on a common scale before the ANOVA. The paper does not say what it
# did for the US-only ANOVA; it z-scored within each slider for the cross-cultural one.
#   "z"     z-score within each slider, across participants, emotions and modalities
#   "range" proportion of each slider's range (0-1)
#   "raw"   raw slider units (bpm then dominates the Slider factor)
# Set this to the rule in your preregistration.
slider_scaling <- "z"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusion rule: replace with the rule you preregistered. Here: music-group participants
  # who failed the sound check (fewer than 2 of 3 note counts correct, after up to 3 rounds).
  # Completing the study already guarantees a saved setting for all five emotions.
  failed_sound <- if ("audio_check_passed" %in% names(complete)) {
    complete$condition == "music" & as.logical(complete$audio_check_passed) %in% FALSE
  } else {
    rep(FALSE, nrow(complete))
  }
  keep <- complete[!failed_sound, ]

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep,
       n_failed_sound_check = sum(failed_sound))
}

# The dependent measure in long format: one row per participant x emotion x slider, for the
# analysed participants.
emotion_settings <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "emotion_setting", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    select(participant_id, condition, emotion, bpm, jitter, scale, interval, updown) |>
    pivot_longer(c(bpm, jitter, scale, interval, updown), names_to = "slider", values_to = "value") |>
    mutate(across(c(participant_id, condition, emotion, slider), as.character),
           value = as.numeric(value))
}

scale_sliders <- function(settings, how = slider_scaling) {
  settings |>
    left_join(slider_ranges, by = "slider") |>
    group_by(slider) |>
    mutate(y = switch(how,
                      z     = (value - mean(value)) / sd(value),
                      range = (value - lo) / (hi - lo),
                      raw   = value)) |>
    ungroup()
}

# The key analysis: Emotion x Slider (within) x Modality (between) ANOVA, Greenhouse-Geisser
# corrected, partial eta-squared, as in the original. Returns one row per term, or NULL until
# each modality has at least two analysed participants with all 25 settings.
key_anova <- function(settings) {
  if (is.null(settings) || nrow(settings) == 0) return(NULL)
  full <- settings |> filter(!is.na(value)) |> count(participant_id) |> filter(n == 25)
  s <- settings |> filter(participant_id %in% full$participant_id)
  per_group <- s |> distinct(participant_id, condition) |> count(condition)
  if (nrow(per_group) < 2 || min(per_group$n) < 2) return(NULL)
  s <- scale_sliders(s)
  if (any(!is.finite(s$y))) return(NULL)  # a slider with no variance yet (tiny pilots)
  fit <- suppressMessages(aov_ez(id = "participant_id", dv = "y", data = s,
                                 within = c("emotion", "slider"), between = "condition",
                                 anova_table = list(correction = "GG", es = "pes")))
  tab <- as.data.frame(fit$anova_table)
  tibble(term = rownames(tab), df1 = tab[["num Df"]], df2 = tab[["den Df"]],
         F = tab[["F"]], pes = tab[["pes"]], p = tab[["Pr(>F)"]],
         N = n_distinct(s$participant_id))
}
key_row <- function(tab) if (is.null(tab)) NULL else tab |> filter(term == "emotion:slider")

# Confidence interval for partial eta-squared by inverting the noncentral F distribution
# (Smithson, 2003). A 90% interval is conventional for eta-squared, since it is bounded at 0.
pes_ci <- function(F, df1, df2, level = 0.90) {
  a <- (1 - level) / 2
  ncp_for <- function(target) {
    g <- function(ncp) pf(F, df1, df2, ncp) - target
    if (g(0) < 0) return(0)
    uniroot(g, c(0, 10), extendInt = "downX")$root
  }
  ncp <- c(ncp_for(1 - a), ncp_for(a))
  ncp / (ncp + df1 + df2 + 1)
}

# Mean setting per emotion x slider with a 95% CI, for the figures.
settings_summary <- function(settings) {
  if (is.null(settings) || nrow(settings) == 0) return(NULL)
  settings |>
    group_by(emotion, slider) |>
    summarise(n = n(), mean = mean(value), se = sd(value) / sqrt(n), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(low = mean - qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * se, high = mean + qt(0.975, pmax(n - 1, 1)) * se)
}

# Side-by-side figure: mean slider position for each emotion, as a proportion of each slider's
# range, for any number of studies in the order given. Studies without CIs (the original
# reports none) are drawn without error bars.
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    left_join(slider_ranges, by = "slider") |>
    mutate(across(any_of(c("mean", "low", "high")), ~ (.x - lo) / (hi - lo)),
           Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           emotion = factor(emotion, levels = c("angry", "happy", "peaceful", "sad", "scared")),
           label = factor(label, levels = slider_ranges$label))
  if (!"low" %in% names(df)) df <- mutate(df, low = NA_real_, high = NA_real_)
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = emotion, y = mean, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
    facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1), oob = scales::squish) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean slider position (share of range)", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r) || nrow(r) == 0) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Emotion × Slider` = "not yet collected",
                  `partial η²` = "", `90% CI` = "", p = ""))
  }
  ci <- pes_ci(r$F, r$df1, r$df2)
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Emotion × Slider` = sprintf("F(%.2f, %.2f) = %.2f", r$df1, r$df2, r$F),
         `partial η²` = sprintf("%.2f", r$pes),
         `90% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci[1], ci[2]),
         p = format.pval(if ("p" %in% names(r)) r$p else pf(r$F, r$df1, r$df2, lower.tail = FALSE),
                         digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original (US)", original_key),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_row(key_anova(emotion_settings(phase1)))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_row(key_anova(emotion_settings(phase2))))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: the Emotion × Slider interaction in the Emotion × Slider × Modality ANOVA on slider settings (Greenhouse-Geisser corrected).")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

I'm interested in musical instruments as expressive tools—and how the various aspects of their design affects people's ability to express different intentions.

Sievers et al. (2012) is a production experiment where a set of five features (rate, jitter, direction, step size, and dissonance/spikiness) are mapped to two different modalities: monophonic melodies and an animated ball. A participant is assigned a modality, and tunes the 5 parameters to generate content that match various emotions. Replicating this study will be helpful for my research program in several ways—it's both a great example of how to study cross-modal mappings between music and movement, and will also have me implement a paradigm that could become reusable infrastructure for future studies.

The authors reported three main results: (a) each emotion was mapped to a unique combination of features, (b) those features were similar for both music and movement, and (c) the common mappings of emotion to music and movement existed cross-culturally. I'm replicating the first of 2 experiments reported in the paper, which is the experiment conducted in the US. I'm aiming to replicate results (a) and (b), both of which come from running multiway ANOVA on the positions of the sliders for each modality and each emotion. The Emotion x Slider interaction is the primary result (original: partial η\^2 = 0.23, though this was pooled across populations, so I might recompute the US-only value from the dataset).

Replicating the experiment will require building an interface where participants manipulate sliders to generate both melodies and simple 3D animations. The studies were not originally run in a web browser, so I will be re-implementing the tech stack from scratch. This will require a non-trivial amount of engineering work, as I'll be implementing both sound synthesis and in-browser 3D rendering systems. The functionality of the programs themselves are quite well documented by the original authors.

The extensions I'm considering are: (i) removing the descriptive natural-language labels for the sliders, since it's possible that participants are mapping emotions directly to the adjectives (e.g. "smoothness" or "rate") and not to the resulting visual/auditory stimuli, and (ii) testing if the results hold with a non-emotion set of concepts. A bigger sample size might also be a useful extension (the original study was N=25 for each condition).

## Methods

### Power analysis

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Report the original effect size, the sample needed for 80%, 90% and 95% power to detect it, and the sample you chose and why. The table below is computed from the original study's numbers entered at the top of this file.

Original effects are usually overestimates, so powering to the original effect tends to produce an underpowered replication. One widely used alternative is to collect 2.5 times the original sample, which gives 80% power to detect an effect the original study had only 33% power to detect (Simonsohn, 2015; Experimentology §10.4). Say which approach you used, and what the course's participant budget allowed.
:::

```{r}
#| label: power
# Power for the Emotion x Slider interaction, from the original partial eta-squared, using the
# usual noncentral-F approximation for a within-subjects effect: f^2 = pes / (1 - pes),
# noncentrality = f^2 x error df, with the original Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon
# (4.81 / 16) applied to both df. Two modalities of equal size.
eps_gg <- original_key$df1 / 16
power_rm <- function(n_total, pes, eps = eps_gg) {
  f2  <- pes / (1 - pes)
  df1 <- 16 * eps
  df2 <- (n_total - 2) * df1
  1 - pf(qf(0.95, df1, df2), df1, df2, ncp = f2 * df2)
}
n_for_power <- function(target, pes) {
  for (n in seq(4, 2000, by = 2)) if (power_rm(n, pes) >= target) return(n)
  NA
}

power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- n_for_power(pw, original_key$pes)
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = n / 2, n_total = n)
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N per modality", "N total"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original Emotion × Slider interaction (partial η² = %.2f), alpha = .05. The effect is very large, so this is not what limits the sample.",
               original_key$pes))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample would be `r two_and_half[1]` in the gain frame and `r two_and_half[2]` in the loss frame (`r sum(two_and_half)` in total).

### Planned sample

I'm planning to sample from US residents on Prolific who are 18+ years old and fluent in English. (The original sample was from Dartmouth college students in a lab, with no other demographics reported.) The participants must be on desktop (not phone or tablet) and able to play audio from their computer.

I'm planning to run 2.5x the original sample, which will be 126 participants total (63 people per modality). I will collect until 63 people in each modality pass the exclusion criteria.

### Materials

The study is run using a computer program that generates both sound and visuals. I replicated the generators for both exactly. A summary is given in the original paper:\
"We created a computer program capable of generating both music and movement; the former as simple, monophonic piano melodies, and the latter as an animated bouncing ball. Both were controlled by a single probabilistic model, ensuring there was an isomorphic relationship between the behavior of the music and the movement of the ball. This model represented both music and movement in terms of dynamic contour: how changes in the stimulus unfold over time. Our model for dynamic contour comprised five quantitative parameters controlled by on-screen slider bars. Stimuli were generated in real time, and manipulation of the slider bars resulted in immediate changes in the music being played or the animation being shown."

There are 5 on-screen slider that control the generation of either the visual or auditory clips, with the labels ("rate", "jitter", "consonance/smoothness", "step size", "direction") copied from the original paper.

Each clip contains 16 events, where the music is monophonic MIDI piano (velocity=110), and movement is a red ellipsoid with eyes where bounce height follows interval size, tilt follows pitch (60 - MIDI note in degrees), and surface smoothness follows interval consonance.

Emotion words are the original five clusters, anchored by "happy", "sad", "angry", "scared", and "peaceful." Audio is synthesized via the Salamander Grand Piano sample library, and the visuals are rendered via a three.js port of the original Processing code, copying the geometry, lighting, and camera position.

### Procedure

After the user completes a consent form and audio/browser check, they are introduced to their assigned modality (either audio or visual/movement). They get unlimited time to practice with the interface, where the sliders are assigned to random values and are freely manipulable.

Then, they are introduced to the study task. There are 5 emotion categories. For each, the user can select it, edit the slider positions, and view/listen to the resulting clip. The user can re-play and re-edit the slider values at any point, and can return to each emotion as many times as they please. The user can do this in any order, and there is no time limit. The user must visit all 5 emotion categories before they finish with the study.

### Analysis plan

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

The analysis strategy, as close to the original as possible: data cleaning rules, exclusion rules, covariates, and the model or test. Original papers often do not spell this out; say where you had to make a choice and what you chose.

**State the key analysis of interest explicitly.** That is the single test your replication stands or falls on, and it must match your preregistration. You can pre-specify additional analyses here too.
:::

**Key analysis of interest.** The proportion of participants choosing the risky program is higher in the loss frame than in the gain frame, tested with a chi-square test of independence on the 2 × 2 table of frame by choice. The effect size is the difference in the proportion choosing the risky program (loss minus gain), with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, if they answered no speeded trial at all (every lexical-decision trial timed out, the signature of a device without a keyboard), or if they answered fewer than 6 of the 8 lexical-decision trials correctly.

### Differences from the original study

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every known difference in sample, setting, procedure, materials, and analysis, one per row. Minimizing differences is the goal, but some always remain. For each one, say whether it is expected to matter, based on claims in the original article or later research on when the effect does and does not appear. The rows below are the demo's real differences and show the level of detail expected; replace them with yours.
:::

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | University students in Stanford and British Columbia classrooms | Adults recruited on Prolific | Possibly. Framing effects have been found in both student and general samples, but their size varies across populations. |
| Setting | Paper questionnaire in class | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer | Unlikely for a single vignette, though attention may be lower online. |
| Wording | "an unusual Asian disease" | "an unusual disease" | Unlikely. The ethnonym is incidental to the manipulation and dated. |
| Design | Between subjects: each participant saw one frame | Between subjects, randomly assigned | No. |
| Response | Circle a program on paper | Click a button | Unlikely. |
| Other tasks | Problems presented alongside other questionnaire items | Followed by a short lexical-decision task used as an attention check | Unlikely: the check comes after the choice. |

```{r}
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Started"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
```

```{r}
  filter(task == "demographics", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
  transmute(
    participant_id,
    age    = map_dbl(resp, ~ as.numeric(.x$age %||% NA)),
    gender = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$gender %||% NA))
  )

if (nrow(demo) > 0) {
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample.")
}
```

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared analysis code under Key statistics (open "Show the analysis code"). Describe anything you did to the data beyond that.
:::

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
settings <- emotion_settings(phase1)
key_tab  <- key_anova(settings)

if (!is.null(key_tab)) {
  key_tab |>
    mutate(across(c(df1, df2), ~ round(.x, 2)), F = round(F, 2), pes = round(pes, 3),
           p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(col.names = c("Term", "df1", "df2", "F", "partial η²", "p", "N"),
                 caption = sprintf("Emotion × Slider × Modality ANOVA on slider settings (scaling: %s), Greenhouse-Geisser corrected. The key term is emotion:slider.", slider_scaling))
} else {
  message("ANOVA not run: it needs at least two analysed participants in each modality with all ",
          "25 settings; there are ", n_distinct(settings$participant_id), " analysed participant(s).")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_key
rep  <- key_row(key_tab)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original (US)"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    rowwise() |> mutate(ci = list(pes_ci(F, df1, df2))) |> ungroup() |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Emotion × Slider` = sprintf("F(%.2f, %.2f) = %.2f", df1, df2, F),
              `partial η²` = sprintf("%.2f", pes),
              `90% CI` = map_chr(ci, ~ sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", .x[1], .x[2]))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size of the key interaction, original and replication.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants in each modality.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  ci <- pes_ci(rep$F, rep$df1, rep$df2)
  includes_orig <- orig$pes >= ci[1] & orig$pes <= ci[2]
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's Emotion × Slider interaction is %s (p %s), partial η² = %.2f, and its 90%% interval [%.2f, %.2f] %s the original estimate of %.2f. ",
    if (rep$p < 0.05) "significant" else "not significant",
    if (rep$p < 0.001) "< .001" else sprintf("= %.3f", rep$p),
    rep$pes, ci[1], ci[2], if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include", orig$pes))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}
    ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Mean slider position for each emotion, as a share of each slider's range: original study (SI Table S1, music and movement pooled; no variability reported) and Phase 1 replication (95% confidence intervals)."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original_means, `Phase 1: replication` = settings_summary(settings))
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so they generate hypotheses rather than test them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-crossmodal
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: do the two modalities choose the same profile for each emotion? Correlation
# across the 25 emotion x slider cells between the music group's and the movement group's
# mean (scaled) settings.
profiles <- if (nrow(settings) > 0) {
  scale_sliders(settings) |>
    group_by(condition, emotion, slider) |>
    summarise(y = mean(y), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = y)
} else tibble()

if (all(c("music", "movement") %in% names(profiles)) && sum(complete.cases(profiles)) > 2) {
  r <- cor(profiles$music, profiles$movement, use = "complete.obs")
  message(sprintf("Exploratory: music-movement correlation of mean emotion profiles, r = %.2f (25 cells).", r))
  profiles |>
    mutate(across(c(music, movement), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
    arrange(emotion, slider) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Exploratory: mean scaled setting (%s) by emotion, slider and modality.", slider_scaling))
} else {
  message("Need analysed participants in both modalities for the cross-modal comparison.")
}
```

Open with one paragraph summarizing the result of the key analysis and your assessment of whether the original finding replicated, partially replicated, or failed to replicate. Base that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the original, not just the p value.

### Commentary

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the replication means, for example whether the differences between your study and the original are definitely, plausibly, or unlikely to be moderators of the result; and (c) any objections or challenges raised by you or the original authors.

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement, Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| \# | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n_per_group <- 150   # planned analysed participants per modality in Phase 2

p1_stats <- if (have_data) key_row(key_anova(emotion_settings(phase1)))
basis_pes <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$pes else original_key$pes
basis_src <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1" else "the original study"

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: partial η² = %.2f", original_key$pes),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: partial η² = %.2f", p1_stats$pes),
                         sprintf("A tenth of the original: partial η² = %.2f", original_key$pes / 10)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_rm(2 * phase2_n_per_group, original_key$pes),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_rm(2 * phase2_n_per_group, p1_stats$pes),
    power_rm(2 * phase2_n_per_group, original_key$pes / 10)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test (Emotion × Slider) at %d per modality, alpha = .05; current basis: %s.",
                                 phase2_n_per_group, basis_src))
```

On the scientific track, specify the test for the new comparison. Name the exclusion rule (unchanged unless it is in the Changes table) and list any exploratory measures.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-results
#| eval: !expr have_phase2
p2_settings <- emotion_settings(phase2)
p2_stats    <- key_row(key_anova(p2_settings))
cat(sprintf("Phase 2: %d started, %d completed, %d analysed.\n",
            nrow(phase2$participants), nrow(phase2$complete), nrow(phase2$keep)))
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {
  ci <- pes_ci(p2_stats$F, p2_stats$df1, p2_stats$df2)
  p_text <- if (p2_stats$p < 0.001) "p < .001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", p2_stats$p)
  cat(sprintf("Key comparison (Emotion × Slider): F(%.2f, %.2f) = %.2f, %s, partial eta-squared = %.2f [%.2f, %.2f].\n",
              p2_stats$df1, p2_stats$df2, p2_stats$F, p_text, p2_stats$pes, ci[1], ci[2]))
}
```
